props.title: The Law West of Tombstone

sections.content: **The Law West of Tombstone** (1938) represents a fascinating entry in RKO Radio Pictures' Western lineup, starring Harry Carey as a charming fraudster who becomes an unlikely frontier lawman. The film follows a pattern established by earlier Westerns like **Law and Order** (1932) but adds elements of comedy that would later influence films like Destry Rides Again (1939). Carey's performance as Bill Barker draws on his extensive silent Western experience, having been a protégé of D.W. Griffith and starring in numerous early frontier films like **Straight Shooting** (1917).

sections.content: The late 1930s marked a crucial transition period for Western films, as the genre evolved from straightforward action-adventures into more nuanced character studies. **The Law West of Tombstone** (1938) bridges this gap, incorporating humor while maintaining traditional Western elements. The film's approach to law and order themes would influence later classics like My Darling Clementine (1946) and **Red River** (1948), though with a notably lighter touch.

Director Glenn Tryon, primarily known for comedies, brings an unusual perspective to the Western genre. His handling of the material creates an interesting contrast to contemporaneous serious Westerns like **The Oklahoma Kid** (1939) and **Jesse James** (1939). The film's blend of humor and frontier justice anticipates later hybrid Westerns like **Support Your Local Sheriff!** (1969). SUBHEAD: Comedy in the Old West

sections.content: The film's importance lies partly in its early integration of comedy into Western tropes, predating the more famous examples like **The Paleface** (1948) and **Cat Ballou** (1965). Harry Carey's performance as the smooth-talking Bill Barker established a template for charismatic Western anti-heroes that would influence characters in films like **Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid** (1969).
